name: Asgad
title: Ancestor of a prominent family after the exile
lifespan: Likely 600–500s BCE (exilic period and early Persian era)
summary: Asgad was the head of a large clan that played an important role in the restoration of the Jewish community after the exile in Babylon. Although biblical sources tell little about Asgad personally, the number of his descendants testifies to the significance of the family. At the first return under Zerubbabel (around 538 B.C.), 1222 of his descendants are listed, and under Ezra's leadership (around 458 B.C.) an additional 110 men returned, led by Johanan son of Hakkoz. Nehemiah's parallel list records 2322 descendants, a difference in numbers that likely reflects textual-critical and recording variations. Asgad's clan also distinguished itself at the sealing of the covenant during Nehemiah's reforms, where they pledged loyalty to the Torah. This participation in several decisive events during the restoration period—from the return from exile to the renewal of the covenant—shows that the family was a supporting force in the renewed community in Jerusalem.

keyEvents.title: Asgad's descendants return with Zerubbabel
keyEvents.description: At the first return from Babylon under Zerubbabel, 1,222 of Asgad's descendants were among those who returned to Judah and Jerusalem.

keyEvents.title: Recorded in Nehemiah's list
keyEvents.description: Asgad's descendants are also listed in Nehemiah's register of those who returned, with a count of 2,322. The difference from the number in Ezra's list may be due to different times of registration or variations in the textual transmission.

keyEvents.title: Further descendants return with Ezra
keyEvents.description: Under Ezra's leadership, even more of Asgad's descendants returned to Jerusalem, led by Johanan son of Hakkoz, with 110 men.

keyEvents.title: Asgad's descendants seal the covenant
keyEvents.description: Representatives from the family of Ashgad were among those who set their seal on the written covenant to follow God's law during Nehemiah's reforms in Jerusalem.

versions.summary: Ashgad was the ancestor of a family that returned from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem. His descendants are mentioned among those who returned under both Zerubbabel and Ezra, and some of them sealed the covenant under Nehemiah.
versions.title: Head of a returning family
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Head of a Returning Family' is functional, but could have been slightly more specific, e.g., 'Ancestor of a family that returned from exile'. Nevertheless, it is acceptable.; [minor] The role 'leader' is somewhat imprecise. Asgad is primarily referred to as a family head/ancestor rather than an active leader. 'Family head' or 'ancestor' would have been more precise. Additionally, 'ancestor' could have been added.; [major] The number 1222 for Asgad's descendants in Ezra 2:12 is incorrect. According to Ezra 2:12 the number is 1222 – this actually matches many texts. However, some Hebrew manuscripts have variants. The number should be verified. The most common number is 1222, so this appears correct.; [minor] The description says 'Johanan, son of Hakkatan' – the Hebrew name in Ezra 8:13 is 'Johanan, son of Hakkatan'. The phrasing 'Hakkatan son' is slightly unusual in Norwegian; 'son of Hakkatan' is more natural.; [major] In Nehemiah 10:15 (Hebrew 10:16) – the reference should be checked. In many Bible editions Asgad appears in Nehemiah 10:15 (some have 10:16 due to verse numbering variations). Neh 10:15 is acceptable, but it could also be verse 16 depending on the verse numbering. Keeping 15 as reasonable.; [major] Footnotes are missing. A profile like this should include at least some footnotes about the meaning of the name, numerical differences between the Ezra and Nehemiah lists, and historical context for the return from exile.; [minor] The final event 'Enumeration among Israel's families' is more a summary/repetition of information already covered by the other events. It adds limited new information and could have been removed or rephrased to avoid redundancy.; [minor] The summary is good, but could briefly mention the interesting numerical difference between the Ezra and Nehemiah lists (1222 vs 2322), which is a known textual critical point.

versions.summary: Ashgad was the ancestor of a large and prominent family that returned from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem. His descendants are mentioned among those who returned under both Zerubbabel (c. 538 B.C.) and Ezra (c. 458 B.C.). The lists in Ezra and Nehemiah record 1,222 and 2,322 descendants respectively, indicating a significant lineage. Representatives from the family were also among those who sealed the covenant to follow God's law during Nehemiah's reforms.
versions.title: Ancestor of a prominent family after the exile
versions.reason: [minor] Asgad himself may have lived significantly earlier than the 5th century BC, since his descendants were already a large clan by the first return in 538 BC. It is more precise to say that his lifespan is unknown, or to state that he probably lived during the exile period (600–500s BC).; [minor] The summary is good but can be improved by clarifying that Asgad himself likely lived during the exile, and that it is his descendants who are the active historical actors. This provides a clearer distinction between the patriarch and the clan.; [minor] The etymological analysis is reasonable, but it should be clarified that 'Gad' as a deity or concept of luck has roots in Semitic religion and that the interpretation is debated among scholars.; [major] In Nehemiah 10:15 (according to Hebrew verse numbering) or 10:16 (in some translations), Asgad is mentioned. It should be verified whether verse 15 is the correct reference. In many translations, it is verse 16 that mentions Asgad among those who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:1–28/29 has different verse numbering). Many texts place Asgad in Neh 10:16.

versions.summary: Asgad was the patriarch of a significant clan that played a prominent role in rebuilding the Jewish community after the Babylonian exile. Although little is known about Asgad personally, sources testify to the large size and influence of his descendants. The clan participated in the return under Zerubbabel (c. 538 BC), and further family members returned under Ezra's leadership (c. 458 BC). The lists in Ezra and Nehemiah record 1222 and 2322 descendants respectively, differences that reflect the complexity of transmitting these records. Representatives from Asgad's family were also among those who sealed the covenant of faithfulness to God's law during Nehemiah's reforms, demonstrating the clan's ongoing commitment to the restored community.
versions.title: Ancestor of a prominent family after the exile
versions.reason: [minor] Neh 7:17 is the correct reference for Asgad in Nehemiah's list. Verified and accurate.; [minor] Ezra 8:13 is the proper verse for Asgad's descendants during Ezra's return. Correct reference.; [major] In Nehemiah 10, the verse numbering for Asgad varies depending on the textual tradition. In the Hebrew text, Asgad is mentioned in Neh 10:16 (v15 in some numberings), but the most common reference counts the covenant list starting from verse 2 (10:1 in some translations serves as a heading). Verse 16 is reasonable but should be verified. Most references cite Neh 10:15 for Asgad. Changed to verse 15.; [minor] The numerical difference between Ezra and Nehemiah is primarily a textual-critical/historical issue, not merely theological. The source category should instead be 'historical' or 'linguistic' to reflect that this concerns text transmission and source criticism.; [minor] The phrasing "Probably the 600–500s BCE (exilic period)" is acceptable, but strictly speaking, the term "exilic period" does not cover the entire 500s, since the exile ended around 538 BCE. A more precise formulation would be "the exilic period and early Persian period."

footnotes.text: The name Ashgad (Hebrew: אַשְׁגָּד) is often interpreted as 'Gad is strong' or 'fortune has come.' It combines an Aramaic element that may mean 'strong/power' with the Semitic divine name or concept of fortune 'Gad.' The etymology is debated among scholars, and the Aramaic component may point to cultural influence from the Babylonian exile period.

There is a notable numerical difference between Ezra 2:12 (1,222 descendants) and Nehemiah 7:17 (2,322 descendants). Such discrepancies between the two lists occur for several families and may be due to different times of registration, scribal variations in the transmission of the text, or the inclusion of different subgroups within the lineage.

The return from Babylon took place in several waves. The first was under Zerubbabel around 538 B.C. following Cyrus's decree, and the second under Ezra around 458 B.C. The fact that Ashgad's descendants participated in both waves suggests that the family was a large and well-organized lineage with considerable influence.

The covenant sealing in Nehemiah 10 represents an important theological act where the leaders of the people formally committed to keeping the Torah. The mention of Ashgad's family among those who sealed the covenant demonstrates the family's continued significance in the restored community in Jerusalem.

1 Esdras (also known as 3 Esra), an apocryphal/deuterocanonical book, also mentions Ashgad's descendants in its parallel list (1 Esdras 5:13), confirming the family's historical importance in exile-era sources and showing that the tradition of this lineage was widely transmitted.

The Cyrus Cylinder, a Babylonian clay cylinder from around 539 B.C., confirms the Persian policy of allowing deported peoples to return home. This policy formed the basis for the Jewish returns, enabling families such as Ashgad's lineage to return to Judah.
